newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's Solidarity steps up shipyard protest.
newsitem.headline: Poland's Solidarity steps up shipyard protest.

text.p: The Solidarity trade union announced a strike alert throughout Poland's northern Gdansk region on Friday, stepping up pressure for government credit guarantees to rescue the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard.

"We urge the government, management of the shipyard and banks... to begin real and not feigned talks about the future of the shipyard and its workers," Solidarity's Gdansk chapter said in a statement after a meeting of its leadership.
The strike alert involves instructing teams of workers to be present around the clock at enterprises where the union is represented.
Meanwhile, two more shipyard workers went on hunger strike, joining four colleagues who have refused food since Wednesday.

Under a protest action launched four days ago, about 100 workers are occupying the Gdansk provincial governor's offices. More than 1,000 of the 5,000 employees still working at the yard have been staging rallies each morning.

The workers want the government to provide guarantees for banks, which would finance the completion of existing contracts to build five ships, while the yard seeks an investor to save the whole business.
Solidarity said it could turn the protest into a strike at selected enteprises if the government fails to extend credit guarantees within a week.

"The strike may be staged if the shipyard loses contracts because the government purposefully delays taking a decision or if no decision is taken soon..., I think within a week," Gdansk Solidarity's deputy head Bogdan Olszewski told Reuters.
He said any such strikes would be conducted in a way that would not harm the enterprises.
But the government says that guarantees are now impossible because no bank is willing to extend credit for the state-owned shipyard, operating under bankruptcy regulations since August.
It says that the protest in the shipyard -- where 17 years ago Lech Walesa set up Solidarity, the then Soviet bloc's first free trade union -- deters potential creditors and investors.
The government, dominated by an ex-communist party, accuses the yard's previous managements of signing unprofitable contracts, under which debts mounted to 415 million zlotys ($148 million).
Many unionists and politicians say that the government, which has helped other state-owned enterprises, is refusing aid for the shipyard because it is a nest of political opposition.
